extracted.intended_audience: writers, essayists, and educated readers interested in moral/philosophical guidance on character and manners (those composing character portraits or reflective essays)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for depicting, recognizing, or cultivating human character and social manners in essays or portraits; prescriptive maxims about how character manifests, how it should be judged, and what gentlemanly manners consist of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is a reserved force which acts directly by presence, and without means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quality is often latent and cannot be fully justified by enumerated facts or deeds; listeners may feel 'something finer in the man than any thing which he said.' Examples: Lord Chatham, Washington, Schiller. Character operates by magnetism and immediate effect on observers rather than by catalogued exploits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent strength exceeds recorded deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest part of certain men's power is latent — 'Half his strength he put not forth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great persons often accomplish by demonstration of superiority and presence rather than by visible contests or a long list of acts; reputation may outrun recorded performance because character anticipates and displaces events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must embody truth and conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective representatives are those 'appointed by Almighty God to stand for a fact' — invincibly persuaded of the fact in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such leaders do not need to consult constituents for every word; they 'are themselves the country which they represent' and therefore make their talent trusted. The ability to carry points depends on being the living embodiment of principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character in commerce: natural probity and public reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'natural merchant' combines probity with insight into the fabric of society, placing him above tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A merchant of true character references standards of natural equity and public advantage, inspiring trust and stable dealings; this habitual reference to fairness makes others wish to do business with him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character overpowers lesser natures by benumbing resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher natures affect lower ones so strongly that the faculties of the lower are locked up and offer no resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influence of a true master can seem magical: his presence spreads a 'river of command' or 'torrent of strong sad light' that pervades others and colors events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and justice as the moral summit
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is the summit of being; justice is the application of it to affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure individual natures transmit their will and truth to others naturally; truth and justice are natural forces that make themselves believed and have primacy in ranking natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as centrality and self-sufficingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Character's face is 'self-sufficingness' — centrality, the impossibility of being displaced or overset; a man of character should give a sense of mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons do not depend on external opinion, possessions, or social flattery; their presence refreshes and stabilizes social intercourse and resists being reduced to trivial conversation or rituals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure character by resistance of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural measure of character is the resistance of circumstances; feeble souls are drawn to events and opinion rather than principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character anticipates moral quality before acts occur; those lacking character 'worship events' and require confirmation from favorable circumstances. True character remains regardless of changing fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectitude yields habitual serenity, not clamor
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectitude is a perpetual victory, celebrated by serenity rather than cries of joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person of rectitude need not seek public applause; serenity is the fixed joy of right living and the proper mark of moral victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions must equal substance ('mathematical' correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our action should rest mathematically on our substance; nothing should be attempted beyond what one's nature and capacity can effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True efficacy arises when enterprise matches ability (Xenophon and the Ten Thousand as example). Efforts that mimic reforms or roles learned only 'by ear and understanding from books' without latent enterprise will be tentative and ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incessant growth and future-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of character show incessant growth; they make others feel a 'controlling happy future' opening before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character appears in the sense that new powers and honors are continually being added; a noble person is always on their road, gaining fresh claims on the heart and advancing beyond past achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: New actions redeem old faults
rubrics_metrics.description: New actions are the only apologies and explanations of old ones which the noble can bear to offer or to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than dwelling on past mistakes or offering explanations, the man of character remedies past lapses by subsequent beneficent action—his future conduct justifies him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence is inexhaustible and not a ledger of deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no pleasure in thinking of benevolence measured only by its works; true charity is inferred from spirit, not from a list of donations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated benefactions (lists of donations) look poor compared to the inexhaustible quality of love; Goethe's account of how he spent his fortune illustrates that true charity is shown in spirit and life, not merely in counted acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: character cannot be imitated
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is nature in the highest form. It is of no use to ape it or to contend with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine moral greatness resists artifice; 'nothing but itself can copy it.' True character should grow without contrivance and not be produced by imitation or publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow perspective — avoid judging from glimpses
rubrics_metrics.description: Character 'wants room; must not be crowded on by persons nor be judged from glimpses... It needs perspective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character may not form rapidly and should not be rashly explained from few occasions or press accounts; give time and breadth to perceive a person's true stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep friendship as evidence of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict relations of amity between virtuous men — profound good understanding after exchange of good offices — is one of life's most satisfying proofs of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joyful, deep intercourse that persists after many services is a relational test: when two virtuous men are each 'sure of himself and sure of his friend,' politics and commerce pale in comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman: truthfulness, autonomous behavior, manhood before gentleness
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions, and expressing that lordship in his behavior, not in any manner dependent and servile...manhood first, and then gentleness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners that mark a gentleman presuppose an inward integrity and self-command; outward politeness without this substratum is insufficient. Gentle behavior should flow from inner force, not from servility to persons or opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners as a compound of spirit: virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, power
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners (the gentleman) are 'made of the spirit, more than of the talent of men' and are a compound result including virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While frivolous accretions may attach to the name 'gentleman,' the lasting social interest in the figure derives from these integrated qualities; manners are the spontaneous fruit of strong character and faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between form (manners) and substance (worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something equivocal in words expressing social excellence because 'the flower and fruit, not the grain of the tree, are contemplated' — manners emphasize outward beauty as the aim in social cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While manners emphasize appearance and proportion (the 'flower and fruit'), the essay urges keeping alive the distinction between mere fashion and the heroic character the gentleman ideally represents — manners should ideally indicate underlying truth and force, not merely surface polish.
